research.abstract: Background Atherosclerotic plaque rupture is the leading cause of fatal atherothrombotic events, including myocardial infarction. Intimal microcalcification is a major determinant of plaque instability, but its pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. The nuclear receptor Rev-erb-alpha regulates lipoprotein metabolism and inflammation. We hypothesized that it modulates atherogenesis by also controlling arterial calcification. Methods To identify regulators of vascular calcification, transcriptomic analysis of CD14+CD16- monocytes from diabetic patients with different calcium scores (ANGIOSAFE cohort) was combined with targeted analysis in calcified and non-calcified atherosclerotic plaques from diabetic and non-diabetic patients (AtheroPortal cohort) and in calcified and non-calcified areas of human endarterectomies isolated by laser capture microdissection (OPAL Cohort). Functional relevance was evaluated in 18-month-old Ldlr-/- mouse and in primary aortic vascular smooth muscle cells after targeting Rev-erb-alpha. Results In ANGIOSAFE (n=668), REV-ERB-alpha expression was lower in classical CD14+CD16- monocytes from diabetic patients with low coronary artery calcium scores. In the AtheroPortal cohort (n=968), REV-ERB-alpha expression was reduced in highly calcified plaques from diabetic patients, and laser capture microdissection confirmed lower expression in calcified compared to non-calcified areas of human endarterectomies. Rev-erb alpha-deficient Ldlr-/- mice displayed accelerated atherogenesis and calcification, with SMCs reprogrammed toward an osteochondroblastic phenotype. In vitro, Rev-erb-alpha preserved SMC identity by repressing IL-1-beta-driven transdifferentiation, notably via Spp1, Osterix and Sox9, and repressed the hyaluronidase Cemip, whose activity degrades hyaluronic acid and promotes intimal calcification. Conclusions Rev-erb-alpha restrains SMC-driven vascular calcification by suppressing osteogenic reprogramming, and may represent a therapeutic target to reduce calcification and cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Salmonella Typhimurium is a versatile foodborne pathogen with a broad ecological range, making it an ideal model to better understand pathogen adaptations that allow them to infect multiple hosts and persist across environments. Here, we analysed 595 genomes of S. Typhimurium representing three food animal sources (bovine, swine, and poultry) and one non‐food animal source (wild birds). We found that S. Typhimurium from food animal sources generally had a more open pangenome and harboured more antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Notably, swine isolates exhibited the most open pangenome and the highest prevalence of ARGs, patterns that were associated with a greater presence of mobile genetic elements, particularly plasmids. Despite similar core genome sizes, S. Typhimurium from different sources displayed distinct patterns of positive selection in the core genome that varied in frequency and targeted functional categories. In contrast, although accessory genome sizes varied substantially across sources, the frequency of positive selection remained similar. Using machine learning, we identified source‐predictive genetic variants, many of which are associated with stress‐response functions. These findings suggest that gain and loss of accessory genes and positive selection acting on core genes support differential adaptation in S. Typhimurium, potentially contributing to its broad ecological range.

research.abstract: Abstract Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription-coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.

research.abstract: Time from symptom onset to first care may be a modifiable determinant of COVID-19 outcomes, but it is rarely quantified in primary care. This retrospective cohort study included all 5,248 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases (RT-PCR or certified rapid antigen test) notified to the national surveillance system (SINOLAVE) by a large family medicine unit of the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) in Leon, Mexico, between April 2020 and April 2021. Pandemic waves were classified using the official IMSS definition. Wave profiles were compared with chi-square tests and Bonferroni correction, and predictors of death were assessed by multivariable logistic regression, with sensitivity analyses adjusting for severity signs at first contact. Of the cases, 53.8% were female, mean age was 41.1 years, and 317 deaths (6.0%) were registered. Median time to first care was 3 days (interquartile range: 2-5). Case fatality was 3.0% among patients presenting within 3 days and 9.1% among those presenting later. Later presentation (> 3 days) was associated with death (adjusted odds ratio = 1.98; 95% confidence interval: 1.47-2.65), but the association was attenuated after adjustment for severity signs at first contact (adjusted odds ratio = 1.20; 95% confidence interval: 0.85-1.69), which were more frequent among later presenters (21.8% vs. 9.3%). From the first to the second wave, fever (76.1% to 56.9%), diabetes (22.8% to 9.6%), and case fatality (10.5% to 4.8%) decreased, whereas anosmia and dysgeusia increased (all p < 0.001). Surveillance data cannot distinguish clinical progression during delay from late presentation of already severe patients. Delay persisted despite universal entitlement to care, indicating that insurance coverage alone did not ensure timely presentation; prospective cohorts measuring severity at onset are needed.

research.abstract: Background: Measles outbreaks are increasing in frequency globally as vaccine coverage decreases. During the 2025-26 Utah-Arizona border outbreak, identifying where and between whom transmission occurred was essential for directing control measures. However, epidemiological data alone are not sufficient to infer transmission patterns. Methods: As part of the local and state-wide outbreak investigation, we conducted amplicon-based whole genome sequencing on residual diagnostic samples from confirmed measles cases collected from June 15, 2025-April 30, 2026. We reconstructed viral dispersal across Utah using Bayesian phylogeographic analyses. We evaluated genetic distance thresholds for identifying recent transmission by comparing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based genetic clusters with known epidemiologic linkages. We then assessed pairwise exposures associated with genetically supported transmission linkage using logistic regression, accounting for network and spatial dependence between pairs. Findings: We generated 509 high-quality whole measles virus genomes from 913 patients. In 2025, most viral dispersal events (67.9%) originated in Southwest Utah and Mohave County, Arizona, where the first cases were reported. By 2026, most viral spread (60.5%) occurred outside of this area. A threshold of 0 SNPs identified epidemiologically linked pairs of individuals with a sensitivity of 77.4% and specificity of 92.3%. Household membership (odds ratio (OR): 219.10, 95% credible interval (CI): 112.66-325.53), participation in the same sport (OR: 15.19, 95% CI: 9.75-20.63), and attendance at the same school (OR: 51.5, 95% CI: 36.38-66.61) were independently associated with transmission linkage. Increasing distance between households was associated with reduced odds of linkage (OR: 0.46: 95% CI 0.44-0.48). Interpretation: Repeated introductions of measles virus from southwestern Utah seeded transmission elsewhere in Utah, with household, school, and sports exposures contributing to onward transmission. Validated genome-based linkage measures can complement contact tracing by helping public health teams identify likely transmission networks and prioritize investigation when resources are constrained.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Although direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and Methods We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee ≥60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded ≥30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. Results In the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. Conclusion An explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

research.abstract: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

research.abstract: Abstract Phylogenetic analyses of molecular evolution often require repeated manual preparation to reconcile taxa, annotate trees, execute models, and summarize results. These steps become increasingly time-consuming and difficult to standardize as the number of taxa, genes, and analytical hypotheses increases. We present HYphlow, an open-source graphical workflow developed in Python that integrates data preparation, trait-based foreground branch assignment, HyPhy execution, and structured result extraction within a single interface. HYphlow reconciles taxon labels across alignments, trees, and trait data; reconstructs ancestral states using parsimony and maximum likelihood; generates alternative foreground annotations; executes HyPhy analyses locally or through portable scripts for high-performance computing; and records analytical decisions and settings throughout the workflow. We evaluated HYphlow using simulations and two published datasets comprising cryptochrome analyses in pigeons and doves and visual opsin analyses in skinks. A name-similarity threshold of 80 reliably recovered simulated spelling variants, while consensus foreground assignment increased precision relative to parsimony or maximum likelihood alone (0.928 vs 0.891 and 0.907, respectively), with a corresponding reduction in recall (0.875 vs 0.921 and 0.918). In the empirical datasets, HYphlow reconciled taxon labels, reconstructed or reproduced foreground hypotheses derived using different approaches, and generated selection results consistent with the principal conclusions of the original studies. HYphlow therefore provides a reproducible framework for carrying comparative molecular evolutionary analyses from independently prepared sequence, phylogenetic, and trait data through branch assignment, model execution, and results summary while retaining researcher control over analytical decisions. HYphlow is freely available under the MIT licence from GitHub at: https://github.com/Schott-Lab/HYphlow .

research.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic inflammation persists in populations with high HIV and tuberculosis (TB) burden, even during suppressive therapy. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is a key mediator, but its correlates beyond infectious status remain unclear in people living with HIV on stable antiretroviral therapy and who are virologically suppressed. We investigated clinical, metabolic, and neurohormonal correlates of TNF-α in a Zambian cohort. Methods This was a cross-sectional study, which included 227 adults recruited from the outpatient medical clinic at Livingstone University Teaching Hospital in the Southern Province of Zambia. Simple and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to determine independent associations with plasma TNF-α levels. Models were adjusted for HIV serostatus and history of TB. Standardized beta coefficients (β_std) were computed to compare the relative magnitude of associations across predictors measured on different scales. Results Among 227 participants, 64.8% were living with HIV (95.3% on integrase strand transfer inhibitor-based ART) and 14.0% had a history of tuberculosis. In multivariable analysis, the strongest independent associations with TNF-α were observed within the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): angiotensin II (β = 1.18 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.51) and aldosterone (β = 0.884 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.47). Living with HIV serostatus was also independently associated with higher TNF-α (β = 2581.1 pg/mL, p = 0.018; β_std = 0.19), while the history of TB was not. Significant metabolic factors associated with TNF-α levels included VLDL (β = 4397.4 per mmol/L, p = 0.038; β_std = 0.16) and triglycerides (β = 1971.6 per mmol/L, p = 0.034; β_std = 0.17). Inflammatory markers sST2 (β = 104.4 per ng/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.31), IL-17 A (β = 1.137 per pg/mL, p = 0.003; β_std = 0.21), and D-dimer (β = 0.037 per pg/mL, p = 0.001; β_std = 0.22) were independently associated, as was plasma potassium (β = 107.3 per mmol/L, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.46). Renin, IL-6, IL-5, hs-CRP, and left ventricular mass were not associated with TNF-α. Conclusion In this high-burden population, RAAS activation was an independent correlate of TNF-α, exceeding the effect of HIV serostatus. These findings support the hypothesis that RAAS inhibition may have anti-inflammatory effects; however, this remains to be tested in prospective and interventional studies.

research.abstract: Background Obesity pharmacotherapy strategies differ in maintenance dose, titration, and lifestyle support, but existing syntheses primarily compare drugs rather than treatment-initiation decisions. We assessed 1-year weight reduction, permanent discontinuation, and incremental dose-related trade-offs while mapping the availability of eligible trial evidence. Methods We searched eight databases and two trial registries through October 2026 for randomised trials (at least 12 weeks) of obesity pharmacotherapy initiation in adults with overweight or obesity. Maintenance, withdrawal, and switching trials were excluded. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed bias and certainty. Bayesian longitudinal network meta-analysis estimated treatment-policy-compatible weight change at 52 weeks. Additional analyses examined discontinuation, dose escalation, titration, lifestyle support, and diabetes-related attenuation. The study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261532130). Findings We included 180 reports from 178 trials (196 randomisation units; 81,014 participants). Only 78 units reached the 1-year evidence layer, 50 informed the primary longitudinal model in adults without diabetes, and 45 of 160 target strategies had non-extrapolated 52-week estimates. Placebo-adjusted weight reductions were greatest with retatrutide 12 mg (-19.80 percentage points, 95% CrI -21.81 to -17.78), tirzepatide 15 mg (-16.87, -18.07 to -15.51), and cagrilintide-semaglutide 2.4/2.4 mg (-16.37, -18.10 to -14.70). Only tirzepatide 15 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg had high-certainty evidence. Thirteen of 32 strategies increased adverse-event-related permanent discontinuation versus placebo; none increased all-cause discontinuation. Five of 22 adjacent dose steps had at least 0.80 probability of adding more than 2 percentage points of weight reduction. Eight 1-year titration contrasts and three trials of randomised lifestyle-support increments were identified. Weight reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes was 62% of that without diabetes (ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.58-0.66). Interpretation Evidence directly supporting 1-year obesity treatment-initiation decisions remains limited. Higher-dose and multi-receptor strategies achieve substantial weight reduction, but certainty and discontinuation trade-offs vary. Better treatment-policy reporting and randomised evidence on titration and lifestyle support are needed.

research.abstract: Background Atrophic gastritis (AG), characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa and glandular atrophy, is an established precursor of gastric cancer (GC) and contributes to iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Although Helicobacter pylori infection is a major environmental determinant, not all infected individuals develop AG or GC, suggesting that host genetic factors influence susceptibility to AG and severe atrophic gastritis (SAG). Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of AG have been limited in size and have not adequately compared anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus strata, leaving potential genetic heterogeneity unresolved. Methods We performed GWAS meta-analyses of AG and SAG, stratified by anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus, involving 214,747 Japanese participants: 75,074 in the discovery phase and 139,673 in the replication phase. Subsequent analyses included genotype-by-serostatus interactions, HLA allele and ABO blood group associations, genome-wide genetic correlations, multi-trait analysis, local genetic correlations, and structural equation modeling. In addition, cross-ancestry meta-analyses were performed using chronic gastritis GWAS data from FinnGen, UK Biobank, and the Million Veteran Program, comprising 1,357,053 participants. Strong associations with seropositive AG/SAG were observed at previously reported GC susceptibility loci, including PSCA and MUC1/MTX1, whereas the MHC class II region showed predominant associations with seronegative AG/SAG. FAP, CCR6, and ATP4A were also found to be associated with seronegative SAG. The identified regions included previously reported GC susceptibility regions MUC1/MTX1, PRKAA1/PTGER4, PSCA, ABO, and MHC. Associations at PSCA and MUC1/MTX1 were replicated at a genome-wide significance level, supporting a shared genetic basis between AG/SAG and GC. Additional AG-associated candidate regions included BMP2, CCDC80, LRRC34, CPEB4, PGC/FRS3, and LMTK2, implicating epithelial regulation, immune responses, transcriptional regulation, and differentiation. A positive genotype-by-serostatus interaction for SAG was observed at MUC1/MTX1. HLA class II alleles, including HLA-DRB1*15:01 and HLA-DQB1*06:02, showed associations with seronegative AG/SAG. The LDSC genetic correlation between AG and GC was 0.529, and the MTAG estimated Omega correlation was 0.694. Local genetic correlation analysis and structural equation modeling further supported shared genetic components. Cross-ancestry integration of seronegative SAG with external chronic gastritis GWAS data identified an additional association at TPTEP1. Conclusions Our findings characterize the genetic heterogeneity of serologically defined AG/SAG according to anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus. They highlight epithelial and mucus barrier-related pathways in seropositive AG/SAG and immune-related pathways in seronegative cases, while also providing evidence of a shared genetic basis between AG and GC. Together, these results clarify the genetic basis of a GC precursor and are consistent with a continuum from chronic inflammation through atrophy to carcinogenesis. These insights may inform prevention strategies and personalized management of the diverse health consequences of AG.

research.abstract: Introduction. Diet quality scores are well-established predictors of cardiometabolic health but compress an individuals food intake into a single dimension, potentially masking dietary variation relevant to disease risk. Whether this hidden variation carries prognostic information has not been tested at scale. Methods. We applied non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to the reported intake of 148 individual foods and beverages from 87,162 UK Biobank participants. We tested the association of NMF-derived intake factors with incident coronary artery disease (CAD), type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) over a median 9.4 years of follow-up using Cox proportional hazards models. We evaluated the prognostic value of the factors beyond diet quality scores using stepwise Cox models and net reclassification improvement (NRI), and characterized their metabolic profiles through metabolome-wide association analyses (MWAS) of 249 circulating metabolites. Results. NMF identified eight reproducible intake factors that were stable across geographically distinct samples. Four factors were significantly associated with incident cardiometabolic disease: a high sugar and processed foods factor was adversely associated with T2D (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.11-1.27) and CKD (HR 1.15; 1.07-1.23), while a plant-based and fish factor was protective for CKD (HR 0.90; 0.84-0.96) and a cheese and whole grains factor was protective for CAD (HR 0.94; 0.90-0.98). The factors improved disease discrimination beyond both diet quality scores ({Delta}C up to +0.0049) and correctly reclassified 8-16% more individuals, whereas adding either score to models containing the factors produced negligible further improvement. The high sugar and processed foods factor was associated with depletion of omega-3 fatty acids and the plant-based and fish factor showed enrichment in polyunsaturated fatty acids. Conclusions. Food-level dietary intake profiling captures clinically relevant variation that established diet quality scores mask, offering a path toward more personalized dietary assessment for cardiometabolic disease prevention.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bedaquiline (BDQ), pretomanid (Pa) and linezolid (LZD)-based (BPaL) regimens have transformed rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment. However, resistance to these drugs is increasingly reported, while longitudinal data integrating clinical, phenotypic and genomic evolution remain limited. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a fatal case of recurrent RR-TB in a 40-year-old South African woman with HIV infection who received BPaL therapy. Following treatment completion, recurrent disease was complicated by pregnancy, treatment interruption and loss to follow-up. She subsequently re-presented with advanced cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and respiratory failure. Despite re-initiation of BPaL, she deteriorated and died from septic shock. Routine drug susceptibility testing, available posthumously, confirmed resistance to BDQ, Pa and LZD. Seven sequential Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected during treatment underwent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing and whole-genome sequencing. All demonstrated phenotypic resistance to the three BPaL drugs. Serial genomic analysis identified progressive Rv0678 diversification associated with a two-fold increase in BDQ MIC, while resistance-associated rrl and fbiC mutations remained comparatively stable despite persistently elevated LZD and Pa MICs. CONCLUSIONS: This case demonstrates the interaction of treatment interruption, delayed resistance detection and continued within-host bacterial adaptation during BPaL therapy. Longitudinal phenotypic and genomic findings revealed distinct resistance trajectories among BPaL drugs, highlighting the importance of treatment retention, timely susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance for preserving BPaL effectiveness.

research.abstract: Abstract In adaptive immunity, antigen receptor specificity and affinity drive clonal selection, but what enables individual innate lymphocytes to gain a selective advantage without rearranged antigen receptors remains unknown. We traced somatic mutations in human natural killer (NK) cells, revealing extensive clonal dominance in cytomegalovirus-associated memory, with individual genetically diversified clones comprising up to 95% of the population, originating early in life and expanding over years. Their genetic evolution demonstrated positive selection of acquired coding mutations, linking somatic variation to NK cell clonal fitness. Among candidate drivers, we identified mutations in the chromatin regulator KMT2D, whose induced deletion in mature NK cells conferred a competitive advantage following infection in vivo. These findings establish somatic evolution as a fundamental mechanism shaping innate immune memory.

research.abstract: DEG (Degradation of periplasmic proteins) proteases are ATP-independent serine endopeptidases found in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes including plants. They are considered to be key regulators of development and stress tolerance in plants. In this study, a comprehensive genome-wide analysis identified 19 serine protease-like DEG family proteins in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.), revealing their structural diversity, domain architecture, and regulatory potential. Physiochemical profiling showed a predominance of acidic isoelectric points (pI), variable protein lengths (169–1083 amino acids), and differential stability indices. Subcellular localization predicted most DEG proteases to reside in the chloroplast, with others distributed across cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisome. Domain analysis confirmed the universal presence of the trypsin domain, with varying numbers of PDZ domains and additional conserved motifs among paralogs. Evolutionary divergence analysis of StDEG genes and their orthologs from six Solanaceae species as well as Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, and Zea mays revealed dN/dS ratios below one for all orthologous pairs, suggesting that StDEG genes have evolved under strong purifying selection and remained highly conserved throughout plant evolution. Gene ontology annotations linked DEG proteases to key biological functions including PSII repair, photoinhibition, and chloroplast organization, alongside protein catabolism and light stimulus response. Promoter analysis revealed an abundance of cis-regulatory elements (CREs), particularly light-responsive motifs, along with hormone and stress-related elements such as ABRE, ARE, and MBS. Expression profiling across eight developmental tissues demonstrated tissue-specific expression patterns, with strong transcript accumulation of selected DEG members in senescent leaf, stolon, shoot apex, and tuber. Interestingly, several splice variants showed unique expression dynamics, including stage-specific and stress-induced activation. Upon exposure to abiotic and hormonal cues, 16 DEG proteases displayed significant transcriptional modulation, particularly under light, ABA, and Zeatin treatments, with notable fold changes reaching up to 26-fold in certain variants. These findings highlight the functional versatility of DEG proteases in potato development and stress adaptation, especially their responsiveness to light and hormonal stimuli. The characterization of these proteases paves the way for future studies on their roles in crop resilience and genome editing applications.

research.abstract: The family Noctuidae includes agricultural pests that vary in geographic distribution and host range. This study analyzed 30 mitogenomes representing 14 noctuid species; Ostrinia nubilalis (Crambidae) served as the phylogenetic outgroup. The genomes contained the typical complement of 37 mitochondrial genes and exhibited conserved gene order, pronounced A + T enrichment, and a preference for A/T-ending synonymous codons. A neutrality regression based on species means revealed a modest positive association between GC3 and GC12 (R 2 = 0.3201; p = 0.03494), although it could not distinguish the respective contributions of mutation and selection. Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian analyses of 13 protein-coding genes (11,229 bp) agreed on 26 of the 28 internal groupings in the maximum-likelihood tree, including a strongly supported Spodoptera clade. Differences in deeper relationships occurred at nodes with limited support. All 13 genes had dN/dS estimates below one (0.00306-0.01691), consistent with purifying selection. Codon usage varied among gene categories, and gene-wise codon bias was not significantly associated with dN/dS. Five crop-associated species with multiple larval host plants and documented long-distance migration- Helicoverpa armigera, Athetis lepigone, Spodoptera litura, S. frugiperda, and Mamestra brassicae -fell below the fitted neutrality regression line. Whether their ecological traits relate to this pattern remains requires broader taxonomic sampling and ecological data in future investigations.

research.abstract: A bstract Understanding the mechanisms facilitating the repeated evolution of traits is a core question in evolutionary biology. While repeated evolution has been observed across many systems, behavioral phenotypes have been less well studied than morphological traits. Migration is a behavioral adaptation to seasonality that has evolved independently in many animals, and repeated gains and losses of migratory behavior have been especially prevalent throughout the diversification of birds. While migratory traits are heritable in many taxa and candidate genes underlying intraspecific variation in migratory behavior have been identified, whether similar genetic changes are responsible for the repeated evolution of migration remains poorly understood. We used a phylogenomic approach to investigate the relationship between variation in candidate genes and migratory propensity across nearly all species in the parulid warbler radiation ( n = 101), a group of songbirds in which migratory behavior has been lost and gained multiple times. Comparisons of candidate gene tree topologies to the parulid warbler species tree revealed cases of discordance, though these were explained by differences in the number of phylogenetically informative sites among genes rather than by elevated genetic similarity among species sharing migratory strategies. Testing models of coding sequence evolution identified sites with elevated dN/dS in five candidate genes, suggestive of positive selection; however, variation at these sites showed no clear association with migratory strategy, nor did we detect recurrent selection across lineages where transitions in migratory behavior most likely occurred. Together, these results contradict the hypothesis that selection on shared variation (ancestral polymorphisms or introgressed alleles) facilitated the repeated evolution of migration in this clade.

research.abstract: The Columbretes archipelago in the Mediterranean is an example of deep isolation and sporadic human interaction during the Holocene. We recovered ancient DNA from 2,600-year-old microfauna and historical museum specimens to investigate the island's extinct fauna. Despite challenging preservation conditions, we successfully recovered mitogenomes from historical Vipera latastei specimens, and partial mitogenomes from snake, skink, and lizard subfossils. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the extinct Columbretes snake as Vipera latastei, sharing a haplotype with the historical specimen and clustering with modern populations from northeastern Iberia, validating its provenance and suggesting a single mitochondrial lineage since isolation. The extinct skink, Chalcides bedriagai, also shows affinities with eastern Iberia. These results point to a vicariant origin for the herpetofauna, likely isolated on the island following sea level rise after the Last Glacial Maximum. Conversely, a 2,600-year-old mouse incisor yielded a Mus musculus mitogenome, indicating Iron Age human-mediated introduction. Additionally, genomic analysis of a 11th-century CE human burial revealed an individual with genetic affinities to the Central Mediterranean and Balkans, highlighting medieval maritime mobility. This study resolves the long-debated Columbretes snake identity, traces biogeographic origins and illustrates the interplay of natural isolation and anthropogenic influence on the island biodiversity.

research.abstract: Abstract Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is associated with altered outcomes in established prostate cancer, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We examined whether whole-body metabolic state and systemic metformin treatment are associated with changes in circulating plasma extracellular vesicle (EV) signaling to prostate cancer cells. Plasma EV-derived miRNAs were profiled in six T2D and six non-diabetic (ND) donors, selected mimics were tested in DU145 cells for effects on transcription of ZEB1 , a master regulator of tumor progression. Recipient cell transcriptional responses to human EV-enriched fractions were also assessed by RNA sequencing using six T2D and two ND donors. DU145 cells were also transfected with plasma EV-derived RNA from high fat diet (HFD)-fed mice with or without metformin treatment. Human miRNA profiling identified miR-192-5p, miR-106b-5p, and miR-29b-3p as candidates with greater than two-fold elevation and nominal P <0.05; none of the 84 assayed miRNAs remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Synthetic miR-192-5p and miR-106b-3p mimics increased ZEB1 , whereas miR-29b-3p had no effect on ZEB1 . T2D donor EV exposure was associated with broad range of aggressive responses, including cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, mitotic, and RHO-GTPase-related pathways. Mouse EV-derived RNA from metformin-treated HFD mice induced lower DU145 migration than RNA from untreated HFD mice (12.23% versus 20.25% mean membrane coverage; n=3 mice/group; Welch P =0.0246). Matrigel invasion analysis showed less invasion for HFD+metformin than HFD alone (4.89% versus 7.89%; n=3 mice/group; Welch P =0.0302). These findings support a strong association between abnormal systemic metabolism and circulating EV signaling to drive prostate cancer progression, together with a metformin-driven reduction in the tumor progression activity of plasma EV-derived RNA. The responsible RNA species and molecular mechanisms will be central to future research.

research.abstract: Zoonotic tuberculosis (zTB), caused by animal-adapted members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), is classically attributed to M. bovis but is increasingly linked to M. orygis across South Asia. Species-level MTBC identification is rarely performed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), leaving the zTB burden poorly defined. Bangladesh has endemic bovine tuberculosis, a growing dairy sector, unpasteurised-milk consumption, and expanding captive wildlife collections, yet the evidence has not been synthesised by diagnostic reliability. This systematic evidence map aimed to collate the evidence on zTB in Bangladesh and to review the diagnostic methods used to identify animal-adapted MTBC species, particularly M. bovis and M. orygis , in livestock, wildlife, and humans. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and BanglaJOL from the 1970s to June 2026; CAB Abstracts, Scopus, and Web of Science were not accessible. Two reviewers independently screened and appraised studies using the JBI checklist, assigning each to a five-level diagnostic evidence hierarchy (Level 1: WGS, phylogeny, RD typing, spoligotyping, or MLVA; Level 5: tuberculin skin test or serology only). These non-comparable tests precluded meta-analysis; therefore, findings are presented as an evidence map. Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria: 24 on prevalence in cattle/buffaloes, 10 on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in cattle, captive wildlife, and humans, and 1 specifically on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in humans. Most livestock studies used non-discriminatory tests (tuberculin skin tests, ELISA, or untyped PCR) and reported non-comparable reactor proportions of 1.2% to 33.7%. The few studies using species-level methods (Levels 1–2) confirmed M. orygis in cattle and in at least seven captive wildlife species, including monkeys, using marker-based molecular assays. Several historical reports of M. bovis were based on non-discriminatory PCR or serology, which cannot reliably distinguish among MTBC members. Human evidence was limited to three studies, including one WGS-confirmed M. orygis case identified through tuberculosis surveillance. In published reports from Bangladesh, M. orygis is the only animal-adapted MTBC member molecularly confirmed at the cattle–wildlife–human interface; existing M. bovis claims lack discriminatory support and require cautious reinterpretation. zTB surveillance should therefore move beyond an M. bovis -only framework and integrate species-level MTBC identification into a staged, resource-appropriate One Health strategy across animal, wildlife, and human health.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sputum culture conversion in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is the most important interim indicator for drug-resistant (DR) tuberculosis (TB) treatment effectiveness. Bedaquiline-based regimens offer the possibility of more effective and less toxic treatment for DR TB. Bedaquiline-based regimens have been adopted as the new standard of care for DR TB, replacing the oto-and nephrotoxic aminoglycosides. We determined the median time to sputum culture conversion (TTCC) and associated factors among RR and MDR TB patients treated with Bedaquiline-based regimens, at Mulago National Referral Hospital, Uganda. METHODS: In a longitudinal type of observational study performed at Mulago Hospital, between January 2020 and June 2023, RR and MDR TB patients' records were reviewed to obtain data on socio-demographic and clinical factors, and TTCC. The study outcome was TTCC, recorded as time from RR/MDR TB treatment initiation to sputum culture conversion, which was defined as at least 2 consecutive negative TB sputum cultures, at least 30 days apart, for a RR/MDR PTB patient who was sputum culture positive at baseline. Analysis for median TTCC was done using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and the log-logistic parametric survival regression model was used to identify predictors for TTCC. research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious pathogen globally despite decades of effective chemotherapy. In 2024, an estimated 10·7 million people developed tuberculosis, including approximately 620 000 people living with HIV (PLHIV), and tuberculosis caused an estimated 1·23 million deaths overall, including approximately 150 000 deaths among PLHIV. Men accounted for more than half of the cases, and children represented a substantial burden, reflecting ongoing transmission and diagnostic gaps. Approximately a quarter of the world's population has been infected with M tuberculosis, with immunological evidence of previous or current infection. This population includes groups at increased risk of progression to tuberculosis disease, particularly those with recent infection, HIV, undernutrition, young age, or other clinical and social vulnerabilities. Following 3 years of COVID-19-related setbacks, global tuberculosis incidence declined modestly (1%) from 2023 to 2024 but remains higher than in 2020 and far off-track to meet the 2025 WHO End TB Strategy milestones. Case detection improved to 8·3 million notifications (78% of estimated incident cases), supported by expanded molecular diagnostics; however, prevalence surveys continue to reveal substantial proportions of bacteriologically confirmed but asymptomatic tuberculosis, highlighting persistent transmission and missed diagnoses. 30 high-burden countries accounted for 87% of cases, led by India, Indonesia, the Philippines, China, Pakistan, Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Bangladesh. M tuberculosis-HIV co-infection remains a major driver of mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. Drug-resistant tuberculosis threatens progress: of 390 000 estimated multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis cases in 2024, only 42% initiated treatment, although treatment success improved to 71%. Tuberculosis-preventive treatment reached 5·3 million people, including 58% of PLHIV and 25% of eligible household contacts, well below global targets. Persistent undernutrition, poverty, HIV, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use, air pollution, migration, and conflict continue to shape tuberculosis epidemiology. With financing at only 27% of global targets, accelerated prevention, proactive case finding, social protection, and sustained political commitment are essential to eliminate tuberculosis.

research.abstract: Abstract The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires – even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades – especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 – exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth–death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

research.abstract: Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical threat to global health security and disproportionately affects children in sub-Saharan Africa. In Nigeria, the burden of multidrug-resistant pathogens in paediatric populations is increasing; however, data from the South-South region, particularly Edo State, remain scarce. This study aims to determine the prevalence, patterns and transmission dynamics of AMR among paediatric patients in Edo State, Nigeria, using a One Health approach that integrates human, animal and environmental health interfaces. Methods and analysis This mixed-methods study will enrol 455 hospitalised children (<18 years) at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH). Clinical (urine, blood, rectal and nasopharyngeal swabs), environmental and animal samples will be collected to isolate and characterise locally recoverable bacterial pathogens prioritised with reference to the WHO 2024 priority pathogen list. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing will be performed using the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method in accordance with Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. Selected clinically or epidemiologically important resistant isolates will be stored at -80°C for possible future molecular characterisation, resources permitting. Key informant interviews with caregivers, healthcare providers and policymakers will explore the systemic enablers and barriers to paediatric AMR stewardship. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive statistics and logistic regression, while qualitative data will undergo thematic analysis guided by Braun and Clarke's framework. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been obtained from the UBTH Health Research Ethics Committee (Ref: ADM/E 22/A/VOL.VII/14831247). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. Findings will inform antibiotic stewardship, strengthen surveillance and guide AMR policy at institutional, state and national levels. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, policy briefs, institutional reports and engagement with national and international health agencies.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future. METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods. RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers. CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Species in the Rosaceae tribe Spiraeeae occupy diverse habitats and vary strikingly in growth form and leaf morphology. Still, no reference transcriptomes have been published for the tribe, and its transcriptome‐level variation is uncharacterized. We generated long‐read (PacBio Iso‐Seq) reference transcriptomes of five species spanning three genera: Petrophytum caespitosum (Nutt.) Rydb., Spiraea lucida Douglas ex Greene, Spiraea splendens Baumann ex K. Koch, Aruncus dioicus (Walter) Fernald var. dioicus , and Aruncus aethusifolius (H.Lév.) Nakai. We then quantified expression across 20 individuals using 3′‐tag RNA sequencing (TagSeq) to characterize expression patterns, ortholog sequence divergence, and gene repertoire. Multivariate analyses (principal component analysis [PCA] and hierarchical clustering) resolved replicates into three groups corresponding to the sampled genera. Because the material combined field‐collected and potted plants, we treat expression comparisons as descriptive and do not attribute them to genetic control of interspecific differences. Pairwise analyses revealed extensive transcriptional divergence between genera, including thousands of differentially expressed transcripts in comparisons such as A. aethusifolius vs. P. caespitosum . Functional enrichment highlighted variation in transport and catabolism, plastid organization, and biotic‐stress responses, implicating both metabolic and organelle‐associated processes. Transcription factor families, particularly bHLH and bZIP, varied most among differentially expressed transcripts. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) recovered modules correlated with species identity; because between‐species variation dominates this dataset, we treat these as descriptive summaries of coexpression structure and do not regard them as independent evidence of species‐specific regulatory programs. Because reads were quantified against a reference assembled from species‐specific contigs, mapping rates were higher within species (70.5%–85.1%) than across species (25.1%–77.0%), and between‐species expression comparisons are interpreted with this asymmetry in mind. Sequence‐level analysis of orthologous transcript pairs indicated that protein‐coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection. A small fraction (2.7%–5.0% of retained pairs) showed Ka/Ks > 1, but these were concentrated at low synonymous divergence, where ratio estimates are unstable; we therefore treat them as screening‐level candidates for rapid divergence, enriched for stress‐response, membrane‐trafficking, and ion‐transport annotations, and we make no claim of positive selection. These results provide a comparative transcriptomic framework for Spiraeeae and identify candidate transcripts and protein‐coding differences for future studies of ecological and morphological variation in Rosaceae.

research.abstract: Abstract Eukaryote-infecting small dsDNA viruses, including those referred to as virophages, polintons, and their relatives, are major constituents of ecosystems across the globe as both agents of mortality and as integrated elements that shape host genome evolution. As the ubiquity of these viruses has become apparent, there have been efforts to organize their diversity into major lineages in order to better understand their biogeography, ecological impact, and evolution. Virophages, polintons, and polinton-like viruses were recently placed in the sub-phylum Polisuviricotina, though efforts to resolve relationships within this sub-phylum have been complicated by the vast diversity of these viruses and the existence of horizontal gene transfer between their genomes. To address these complications, we have used a gene profile occurrence based method of phylogenetic tree construction to aid in comparative genomic analysis of Polisuviricotina . We find that mosaicism is common within Polisuviricotina , in particular, reassociation of replication modules and morphogenic modules occurs throughout major Polisuviricotina groups. In addition to mosaic exchanges of full replication modules, we also observe extensive domain swapping within some replicases, indicating that mosaic recombination occurs on both the genome and subgenic level in these viruses. Analysis of individual replication modules suggests that they may be capable of some level of autonomous mobility, partially decoupling their evolution from the morphogenic module. This model helps explain the high levels of mosaicism in these viruses and has implications for the mechanisms through which small dsDNA viruses evolve.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) contributes significantly to the global tuberculosis burden, yet treatment response and drug resistance remain poorly characterized. India, a high- tuberculosis burden country, faces growing challenges of delayed diagnosis, treatment and drug-resistant tuberculosis, particularly in extrapulmonary forms. This study evaluated early clinical response to therapy and identified factors associated with rifampicin resistance among patients with EPTB. A prospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care centre in central India between 2018 and 2024. A total of 532 patients with microbiologically confirmed EPTB, based on the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, were included. The study collected baseline demographic, clinical, and laboratory data. Clinical response at 8 weeks was assessed using standardized criteria. Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified factors associated with slow clinical response and rifampicin resistance. A total of 5,764 presumptive EPTB samples were tested using the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. Among these, 532 patients had confirmed EPTB. Rifampicin resistance was detected in 36 patients (6.7%), while 496 patients had rifampicin-sensitive disease and were included in the response analysis. Among these patients, 113 (22.8%) demonstrated slow clinical response. Slow response showed independent association with HIV co-infection, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, prolonged symptom duration, and non-lymph node disease, particularly abdominal and genitourinary tuberculosis. Socioeconomic factors, such as rural residence and lower educational status, also showed independent association. Elevated inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, showed independent association with slow clinical response. Rifampicin resistance showed independent association with previous tuberculosis, HIV infection, male sex, and disseminated disease. A significant overlap existed between delayed clinical response and drug resistance, as rifampicin resistance occurred more frequently among slow responders than among responders (12.3% vs. 4.1%, p = 0.002). Nearly one-quarter of patients with EPTB demonstrated delayed clinical response at 8 weeks. Both host-related and disease-related factors showed association with treatment response, while rifampicin resistance showed strong association with prior tuberculosis and immunosuppression. The overlap between slow clinical response and drug resistance highlighted the importance of early molecular diagnostics and targeted clinical monitoring in high-risk patients.

research.abstract: Abstract We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories—Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis—targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 ≤ 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). From a data-engineering angle, the pipeline is productionizable with lineage, feature registries, and continuous integration to guard against silent regressions when updating models or data; from a data-science angle, the benchmark provides baselines and analyses that foreground feature alignment and architectural suitability as first-order concerns, inviting ablations on multimodal objectives, retrieval-augmented encoders, and uncertainty-aware decoding. Overall, RadMultiBench highlights that state-of-the-art status in general V-L domains does not translate automatically to high-stakes clinical tasks, and it furnishes the tooling and evidence base needed to develop robust, clinically viable multimodal systems.

research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

research.abstract: Abstract Gene copy-number mutations are frequent and prevalent yet often overlooked. While initially considered to be the neutrally evolving raw material needed for the emergence of new genes through the process of gene duplication and divergence, recent technical advances and renewed interest start to unravel a fundamentally different picture for duplications in bacteria: rather than being neutral, duplications have strong direct and indirect fitness effects, and rather than giving rise to evolutionary novelty through protein family expansions, duplications allow to transiently simply make more of the same. Tandem duplications arise at frequencies orders of magnitude higher than single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and they collapse at an even higher rate still. Understanding the biological idiosyncrasies of copy-number mutations is pivotal to understanding their fundamental role in bacterial evolution. Having multiple copies of a gene influences its evolutionary dynamics in surprising ways, slowing down divergence, acting along with purifying selection as a force of conservation, and facilitating “bet-hedging” in fluctuating environments or under diversifying selection. Paying careful attention to structural variation in genomic sequence analyses will yield a more comprehensive understanding of bacterial evolution, especially when it comes to the emergence of novel bacterial lineages, such as human pathogens.

research.abstract: Characium and Characium -like algae represent a taxonomically challenging group within Chlorophyceae. Due to their high phenotypic plasticity and convergent morphology, their true evolutionary relationships have long remained unresolved, and the lack of genomic resources has further hindered taxonomic revision. We sequenced and assembled seven complete chloroplast genomes from Characium and morphologically similar taxa and documented their detailed cell morphology. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that while most genomes retained the typical quadripartite structure, they exhibited significant structural variation, including gene rearrangements and diverse IR expansions/contractions. Furthermore, phylogenetic analyses based on 64 protein-coding genes successfully resolved the long-standing taxonomic ambiguity of Characium and Characium -like algae, placing the strains into three distinct, well-supported clades within Sphaeropleales and Volvocales. The synteny patterns and DCJ distances were consistent with the phylogeny: closely related species showed largely conserved gene order and low DCJ distances, whereas more distant lineages exhibited extensive rearrangements and higher distances. Branch-site tests identified a small set of positively selected genes, mainly related to photosynthesis, proteolysis, and plastid gene expression, suggesting that adaptive processes may have contributed to chloroplast genome diversity in these algae. This study establishes the first clear phylogenomic framework for these lineages, revealing distinct evolutionary patterns of gene loss and structural rearrangement that align with the newly resolved clades. It also provides an important basis for advancing studies on chloroplast genome evolution within Chlorophyceae.

research.abstract: Introduction: Brain-predicted age, estimated from structural MRI data, is a machine-learning biomarker of biological brain aging. Greater brain age gap (BAG) indicates advanced brain aging and is associated with cognitive decline and mortality. Cardiometabolic risk factors, including elevated blood glucose, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, and cholesterol, increase risk of cognitive impairment and dementia in aging. Their relationship with BAG in severe obesity remains poorly characterized despite increased prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors among this population. Methods: T1-weighted MRI data from 97 adults (BMI 35-73) were used to calculate BAG using ENIGMA and Pyment brain age models. Associations between BAG and HbA1c, BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were examined using multiple linear regression and MM‑estimation robust regression, adjusting for age, sex, and race. Post hoc analyses stratified models by clinical HbA1c cutoffs (normoglycemic, prediabetic, diabetic). Results: Higher HbA1c was associated with greater BAGENIGMA (B = 1.58, p = .014) and BAGPyment (B = 0.93, p = .013) in linear regression models. In robust models, HbA1c remained significantly associated with BAGENIGMA (B = 1.70, p = .002) but not BAGPyment (B = 0.71, p = .13). BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were not associated with BAG in either linear or robust models. HbA1c was associated with greater BAGENIGMA (B = 2.15, p = .01) and BAGPyment (B =1.21, p = .04) in those at or above prediabetic levels and with BAGENIGMA (B = 2.49, p = .047) in those with diabetes. Conclusions: Elevated HbA1c is associated with accelerated brain aging in individuals with severe obesity. BAG was not associated with BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, which may reflect the restricted BMI range inherent to the sample with severe obesity.

research.abstract: Abstract Comparative transcriptomic datasets are increasingly used to investigate the molecular basis of phenotypic diversification across species. However, finding genes that are differentially expressed (DE) between lineages remains challenging, for two main reasons. First, the random evolutionary drift can blur the signal left by lineage-specific shifts in mean expression, and induces phylogenetic correlations that, if ignored, can widely inflate the False Discovery Rate (FDR), i.e., the amount of spuriously detected genes. Second, DE analysis from RNA-Seq data involves multiple testing on many genes for a small number of individual measurements with high noise, and requires dedicated statistical tools. Traditional DE tools, such as limma, and classical Phylogenetic Comparative Methods (PCMs), such as the Expression Variance and Evolution (EVE) model, are both designed to tackle one of these two challenges alone, but both fail in the context of inter-species RNA-Seq data. In this work, we present phyloDE, a new tool for inter-species DE, that aims at taking the best from both approaches. On simulations based on a recently published four-species rodent dataset, we show that, contrary to other methods, phyloDE correctly controls the FDR in all settings, while keeping a reasonable power. When reanalyzing the empirical dataset, phyloDE discovers more DE genes that exhibit consistent changes in their cis-regulatory landscape compared to EVE in all the experimental settings. The method is implemented in R, with an interface inheriting from limma.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Purpose Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) covers multiple drug resistance-associated regions, but drug-organized reports can duplicate variants across drugs and disperse a patient's variants. Through nomenclature standardization and cross-drug deduplication, we reconstructed nonredundant patient-level variant profiles and characterized multigene co-occurrence, molecular variant complexity, and reported frequency patterns. Patients and methods This single-center retrospective descriptive study included each patient's earliest eligible mutation-positive tuberculosis tNGS report from 2024-2025. The analysis dataset comprised report-derived information and did not include raw sequencing data or systematically paired phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) results. Variants were standardized using the 2023 World Health Organization catalogue, H37Rv coordinates, and Human Genome Variation Society recommendations. Duplicate patient-gene-variant records were collapsed into unique patient-variant events while retaining drug annotations. Eight mutually exclusive, exhaustive combinations were defined from RIF (rpoB), INH (katG and/or inhA), and FQ (gyrA and/or gyrB) axes. Results Fifty-seven patients contributed 180 unique patient-variant events involving nine genes and 56 standardized variants. rpoB (84.2%) and katG (64.9%) were the leading genes. The leading variants were katG p.Ser315Thr (63.2%), rpsL p.Lys43Arg (29.8%), and rpoB p.Ser450Leu (26.3%), which together accounted for 37.8% of all events; 33 of 56 variants occurred in only one patient. Seven of the eight RIF/INH/FQ combinations were observed. RIF+/INH+/FQ- was most common (31/57, 54.4%), whereas RIF+/INH+/FQ+ had the highest median numbers of genes and variants (both 5.0). Twenty-three events in 16 patients had reported frequencies below 100%, and pncA- and gyrA-associated events accounted for 60.9%. Conclusion In this mutation-positive cohort, patient-level reconstruction integrated annotations of the same variant across drugs and characterized hotspots and a long tail of variants, multigene co-occurrence within RIF/INH/FQ combinations, and report-derived frequency patterns. This traceable data structure may support laboratory report review and future genotype-phenotype studies.
