research.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h 2 = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport ( SLC17A6 ) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR = 1.05, 95% CI 1.02—1.08, p = 0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.

research.abstract: Abstract Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozens to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.

research.journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
research.abstract: Abstract Bombay duck (Harpadon nehereus), once a minor by-catch in the East China Sea, has bloomed into a dominant species, altering marine ecosystems. This study explored the genomic basis of its mysterious recent success via chromosome-level genome assembly, comparative and population genomics. The genome assemblies of H. nehereus and its closely related outgroup species Saurida undosquamis were of good quality, showing a 96.7–96.8% Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologues completeness. Population resequencing supports a single panmictic population throughout the coast of China. Expanded gene families and genes under intensified and positive selection are related to osmoregulation, hypoxia tolerance, immune function and reproduction. Recent selective sweeps are mostly related to immune response. These molecular signatures are consistent with long-term adaptations to a hypoxic, polluted and fluctuating environment. These findings suggest that species genomically preadapted to environments affected by global change can suddenly become new native invaders.

research.abstract: Remipedes are enigmatic blind, venomous crustaceans endemic to anchialine cave ecosystems (aphotic, hypoxic subterranean environments) and occupy a pivotal phylogenomic position within Pancrustacea as the sister group to Hexapoda. A high-quality genome assembly has long proven elusive for this taxon, due to accessibility challenges and the fragility of remipedes when removed from their habitat. Here we present a highly contiguous, chromosome-level genome assembly for the remipede Xibalbanus tulumensis (Xibalbanidae) spanning 8.05 Gb on 30 chromosome-scale scaffolds, placing it among the largest arthropod genomes reported to date. The protein-coding gene repertoire was highly conserved, with over 97% of arthropod orthologs recovered, and microRNA surveys showed a high level of completeness (94%) relative to pancrustacean genomes. Genome expansion appears to be driven primarily by proliferation of intronic and repetitive elements, which comprise ~71% of the genome. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive gene family turnover, with relatively few families showing lineage-specific expansions and contractions. Venom-associated gene families included the remipede-specific Xibalbins, while significant expansion and episodic positive selection affected other venom-associated gene families. Comparative analysis of macrosynteny revealed that the remipede genome retains the signature of ancient fusion-with-mixing events that unite Pancrustacea and Allotriocarida, with considerable similarity in the chromosome architecture of remipedes and basally branching insect orders. Our findings provide the first genomic framework for Remipedia and reveal a highly expanded, repeat-rich genome that retains deep phylogenetic signals in its architecture, despite being adapted to a highly unusual environment.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Spondylodiscitis is an infectious condition involving the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies. Although Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are the most common pathogens, cases caused by Gram-negative bacilli are relatively rare. Enterobacter hormaechei is an exceptionally uncommon etiologic agent in this context. Case presentation A 69-year-old Turkish male with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of prostate adenocarcinoma in remission, with no active immunosuppression, presented with lower back pain and elevated inflammatory markers. Initially suspected to have metastatic spinal involvement, spinal MRI revealed spondylodiscitis at the T12–L1 level. Microbiological evaluation of the needle biopsy specimen yielded Enterobacter hormaechei . Species-level identification was established by culture and MALDI-TOF MS, with off-label syndromic PCR testing (BIOFIRE ® Joint Infection Panel) providing supportive concordant results. The patient was successfully managed with surgical intervention and appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Discussion Spondylodiscitis due to Enterobacter hormaechei remains exceedingly rare. This case highlights the importance of considering atypical Gram-negative organisms in spinal infections and underscores the value of advanced microbiological methods for accurate species-level identification.

research.abstract: Summary Two otherwise healthy patients from Colombia, now aged 30 and 38 years, developed pulmonary tuberculosis due to inherited, complete TNF deficiency at the ages of 19 and 18 years. We report here a previously healthy Iranian patient with inherited complete TNF deficiency who was diagnosed with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB between 10 and 15 years of age. The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function. Despite normal myeloid and lymphoid subset development, the patient’s primary leukocytes do not secrete detectable amounts of TNF. As in the TNF-deficient Colombian patients, the respiratory burst of GM-CSF-derived macrophages is impaired. Our findings expand the spectrum of TB phenotypes in patients with TNF deficiency and confirm that TNF is essential for immunity to M. tuberculosis in humans but apparently redundant against many other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.

research.abstract: Background Cardiac arrhythmias may remain unrecognized in adults with chronic disease. Established risk scores primarily address atrial fibrillation. Objective To develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)–based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Methods We retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018–2025) from one healthcare organization among adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, or coronary artery disease. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared. XGBoost was selected using internal validation, reduced to 30 features using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated in a holdout set with data ending one day before the index date. Sensitivity analyses excluded information recorded within 30, 90, or 180 days before the index date. An atrial fibrillation/flutter-specific analysis compared XGBoost with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF. Results Among 30,356 patients, 6,835 (22.5%) had a qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis. In 3,051 holdout patients, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.894 (95% CI 0.879–0.908) and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.792 (95% CI 0.763–0.822). At a 0.5 threshold, sensitivity was 0.564, specificity 0.971, and precision 0.857. AUROC remained 0.896–0.897 across earlier cutoffs. In the common score-calculable atrial fibrillation/flutter subset ( n = 2,436), AUROCs were 0.883 for XGBoost, 0.712 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.554 for HARMS 2 -AF. Conclusions XGBoost demonstrated strong internal discrimination for documented arrhythmias. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

research.abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global infectious disease, and novel host-derived biomarkers are needed to improve diagnosis. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are promising biomarkers due to their stability and immune regulatory functions; however, clinically validated TB-associated miRNAs remain limited. This study aimed to identify circulating miRNAs associated with active pulmonary TB. Methods This study included 90 participants: active pulmonary TB (n=30), cured TB (n=30), and healthy controls (n=30). Candidate miRNAs were screened by pooled plasma miRNA profiling and further examined using three publicly available miRNA datasets. Circulating miR-26b-5p was quantified by RT-qPCR. Associations with active TB status were assessed using logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was evaluated by ROC analysis. Putative miR-26b-5p target genes and enriched pathways were explored using bioinformatic analyses. Results Microarray screening identified 108 candidate miRNAs, and cross-dataset analysis identified miR-26b-5p as the only overlapping candidate with consistent downregulation. Circulating miR-26b-5p was lower in active TB and higher in the clinically cured group. It remained associated with active-TB status after adjustment for BMI and PLR. miR-26b-5p showed an AUC of 0.867, while the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.956. Bioinformatic analysis identified 74 putative genes, with EP300, GSK3B, and PTEN as network hubs and PI3K-Akt among the enriched pathways. Conclusion Circulating miR-26b-5p was associated with active pulmonary TB and showed preliminary discriminatory value, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate host-response marker.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Observational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls. Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect. No large observational study has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We aimed to estimate this effect on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID among adults with T2D in England. Research design and methods Using OpenSAFELY-TPP linked NHS electronic health records, we conducted a population-based cohort study with a landmark new-user design. Adults aged 18-85 years newly diagnosed with T2D (August 2018-August 2019) were classified as starting metformin monotherapy within 6 months or not starting any antidiabetic drug, based on prescription data. Follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis and before the UK pandemic (avoiding immortal time) for up to 2 years. We estimated intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects using weighted Cox and pooled logistic regression, with negative (bone fracture) and positive (diabetes-related death) control outcomes. Results Of 52,341 eligible people, 19,599 (37.4%) started metformin. For COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, the maximally adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of metformin versus no antidiabetic was 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.35; 2-year risk difference 0.36%, 95% CI 0.09-0.62; intention-to-treat). The per-protocol HR for COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96-1.29). The Long COVID estimate was imprecise (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83-2.33; intention-to-treat). For bone fracture (negative control) the estimate was null (HR 1.00), but for diabetes-related deaths (positive control) it was elevated (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09-1.81), indicating unmeasured confounding. Conclusions The risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding. These findings align more closely with randomised evidence than earlier prevalent-user studies and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for COVID-19 prevention in newly diagnosed T2D. What is already known on this topic Observational studies and their meta-analyses have consistently reported 30-40% lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, yet most used prevalent-user designs that compare long-term survivors with mixed control groups and can overstate benefit. Randomised trials suggest little or no effect on mortality. What this study adds Using a new-user design in more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding rather than harm. How this study might affect research, practice or policy These findings align with randomised evidence and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for preventing severe or Long COVID in people with T2D. They also illustrate how new-user designs can reconcile discrepant observational and trial results and should be prioritised in future drug-repurposing studies. Lay summary Metformin is a medication commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, some studies suggested it might also protect against severe COVID-19, but many such studies had design limitations that could have made metformin look more beneficial than it truly is. In this study, we used NHS health records from over 52,000 adults in England who were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes to examine whether starting metformin shortly after diagnosis reduced the risk of being hospitalised or dying from COVID-19, being diagnosed with COVID-19. We found no evidence that starting metformin protected against any of these outcomes, although the effect on long COVID was imprecisely estimated. Our findings are consistent with results from clinical trials and suggest that metformin should not be expected to prevent severe COVID-19 in people with type 2 diabetes.

research.abstract: **Background:** Cardiovascular risk factors have changed in the United States, but trends in prevalence, management, and predicted risk through the post-pandemic period remain incompletely characterized. **Methods:** We analyzed 11 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) periods (1999-2000 through 2021-2023) among 60,199 nonpregnant adults aged 20 years or older. Survey-weighted regression assessed age-standardized trends, subgroup differences, and measurement-change sensitivity. We assessed awareness, treatment, and control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. PREVENT equations estimated 10- and 30-year risks among adults without self-reported cardiovascular disease (CVD). **Results:** Obesity increased from 47.4% to 57.2% (odds ratio [OR] per decade, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16-1.30), with class III obesity more than doubling (4.7% to 9.7%). Diabetes increased from 8.2% to 12.7% (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19-1.34), while current smoking declined from 24.4% to 14.9% (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.71-0.81). Hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and prior CVD showed no significant linear trends, although mean systolic blood pressure (BP) (124.2 to 120.2 mm Hg) and total cholesterol (203.6 to 188.1 mg/dL) declined, alongside improvements in other lipids. Hypertension and dyslipidemia awareness and treatment increased, but BP control peaked at 32.5% in 2013-2014 before declining to 21.5%, while LDL cholesterol control rose from 17.0% to 34.2%. Diabetes awareness increased, but treatment trends were nonsignificant. Glycemic control peaked at 51.2% in 2003-2004 before declining to 41.9% (P for nonlinearity < 0.001). Predicted 10-year total CVD risk declined from 5.66% to 5.28%; atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk declined by 0.16 percentage points per decade (95% CI, -0.22 to -0.09), while heart failure (HF) risk increased by 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03-0.17). Their 2021-2023 estimates were nearly identical (3.20% and 3.19%, respectively); 30-year risks showed similar divergence. **Conclusions:** Improvements in smoking, blood pressure, and lipids coexisted with rising obesity and diabetes, declining blood pressure control after earlier gains, and divergent predicted ASCVD and HF risks.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The 2023 American Heart Association cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) staging framework supports risk stratification, but evidence on guideline-level physical activity across stages remains limited. Methods We emulated a target-trial protocol using NHANES 2007-2018 and National Death Index linkage through December 31, 2019. Adults aged 20 to 79 years with CKM stages 1 to 4, estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , complete activity data, no cancer history, and eligible follow-up were included. Baseline activity was classified as meeting or not meeting the guideline. Within-stage propensity-score weights were used in weighted Cox models. All-cause and cardiovascular mortality were the primary and secondary outcomes; 5-year risks used weighted survival curves, with competing-risk cumulative incidence also estimated for cardiovascular mortality. Results Among 19,654 participants, 1,190 all-cause deaths occurred during 134,037 person-years. Baseline attainment was associated with lower all-cause mortality overall (HR, 0.774; 95% CI, 0.675-0.888). Stage-specific HRs were 1.030, 0.803, 0.642, and 0.727 for stages 1 to 4, respectively; estimates were nonmonotonic. Five-year risk differences were +0.040, -0.830, -1.790, and -3.840 percentage points; only the stage 4 interval excluded the null. Cardiovascular mortality showed a similar overall cause-specific association (HR, 0.707; 95% CI, 0.547-0.914). Conclusions Observed baseline guideline attainment was associated with mortality in this observational target-trial emulation. The findings are consistent with current physical activity recommendations but do not estimate the effect of an activity-promotion intervention; prospective trials are needed to establish clinical benefit. Research Perspective What Is New? In a nationally representative US sample, observed baseline attainment of the physical activity guideline was associated with lower all-cause mortality overall, while stage-specific relative associations were nonmonotonic and five-year absolute differences were imprecise except at CKM stage 4. What Question Should Be Addressed Next? Future research should determine whether these stage-specific observational patterns are reproducible across populations and should use prospective intervention designs to investigate the mechanisms and potential clinical relevance of activity associations across CKM stages.

research.abstract: Abstract Sugar beet (Beta vulgaris ssp. vulgaris) is a major global source of sucrose. Domestication and a history of breeding have shaped the distribution of deleterious mutations across the genome. Accurately resolving these variants offers a compelling avenue to accelerate crop improvement through breeding or genetic engineering. We combine three evolutionary methods to identify putatively deleterious derived mutations: angiosperm-wide DNA language deep learning model (PlantCaduceus), fine-scale evolutionary rates from Amaranthaceae plant family sequence alignments using PAML and PhyloP. We defined a high-confidence set of ∼5k deleterious variants enriched for alleles under negative selection. We then evaluate these deleterious mutations across a multi-study panel of more than 1,900 whole-genome sequenced wild and cultivated beet accessions. We found that domesticated beet accessions exhibit higher deleterious load relative to wild maritima, yet sugar beet carries significantly fewer deleterious variants than other cultivated beet crops. Historical trends show a decline in genetic load across more than a century of sugar beet entries in the US NPGS, likely reflecting sustained purging during modern breeding. This combinatorial method of leveraging evolutionary conservation reveals how deleterious mutations have shaped sugar beet breeding history and provides potential targets for future selection, causal-variant discovery, and precision genome engineering.

research.abstract: Abstract Biological interactions involving host-associated fungi are driven by chemistry shaped over evolutionary time. For antagonistic fungi, specialization often involves acquiring genes for novel secretions—including proteins and specialized metabolites—that mediate nutrient acquisition and host defense interactions. Here, we conducted a phylogenomic investigation of Sympodiorosea, ascomycetes commonly found in basal fungus-growing ant gardens. While Sympodiorosea and related genera (Escovopsis, Luteomyces, Manidigitorum, Escovopsioides) are canonically viewed as virulent mycoparasites, non-virulent species may also emerge within these attine-associated fungi. We explored genomic variation in Sympodiorosea to assess potential alternative lifestyles, focusing on the diversity and evolution of metabolic genes. Our study revealed a constrained selective landscape across the Sympodiorosea genome. However, outcomes of in vitro host interactions were diverse and predictable based on the antagonist's ant-species-of-origin, suggesting functional diversification. Phylogenomics indicated that gene gain/loss events in carbohydrate-active enzymes and specialized metabolism drive this diversification. Although selection acts intensely on metabolism-related genes overall, specific metabolic genes experience diversifying selection, indicating their critical role in host associations. Furthermore, Sympodiorosea exhibits protease gene expansions and contractions discordant with a strictly mycoparasitic lifestyle, suggesting either an alternative lifestyle within ant gardens or recent evolution from other niches. These results provide novel insights into fungal genome evolution and the chemistry of the fungus-growing ant symbiosis.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

research.abstract: Purpose: Tinnitus is a common and heterogeneous condition whose genetic architecture remains poorly defined and whose definition varies across studies. We asked which common genetic variants are associated with tinnitus, to what extent genetic associations are shared across heterogeneous tinnitus definitions, and in which brain cell populations tinnitus heritability is concentrated. Methods: Genome-wide association meta-analysis of 19 independent population-based cohorts from Europe and the United States (hereby named EARGEN), comprising 961,085 adults of European ancestry (75,584 tinnitus cases and 885,501 controls). Tinnitus was defined by self-report in 17 cohorts and by diagnostic codes in two. Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) based heritability and genetic correlations were estimated by linkage disequilibrium score regression, genes were mapped by gene-based association together with positional and expression quantitative trait locus mapping. Heritability enrichment was tested by stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression across 31 brain cell superclusters derived from post-mortem human brain donors, and across the 461 cell clusters that compose them. Enrichment was tested for replication in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under a self-report definition (114,325 cases, 201,343 controls) and a diagnostic-code definition (77,601 cases, 310,953 controls). Results: Five independent loci reached genome-wide significance (p < 5 x 10-8) on chromosomes 2, 8, 12, 13 and 16, two of which (rs10877884 and rs2147632) have not been reported previously. SNP-based heritability was 0.0137 (SE = 0.0009) on the observed scale and 0.0535 (0.0036) on the liability scale. Genetic correlations were significant with hearing loss, anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, chronic pain, and four further psychiatric, sleep and vestibular traits. Three superclusters showed a suggestive enrichment in the midbrain-derived inhibitory neurons, amygdala excitatory neurons, and medial ganglionic eminence interneurons at a false discovery rate (FRD) of 0.067, the two latter of which reached significance in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under the diagnostic-code definition (0.030 and 0.006). At cluster resolution, the amygdala excitatory cluster was found significant (z = 4.82, false discovery rate = 3.3 x 10-4), whereas none of the ascending auditory relay cluster were found enriched (z [≤] 1.71, false discovery rate [≥] 0.21). Conclusion: Tinnitus-associated common variation concentrates in limbic and cortical neuronal populations rather than in the ascending auditory pathway. The predisposition to tinnitus therefore appears to be central and largely non-auditory in origin. The small number of genome-wide significant associations obtained despite a large sample emphasizes the need for more detailed and standardized phenotyping focusing on the tinnitus disorder.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as “dead‐end hosts.” Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

research.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) results from acquiring mutations or genes that allow microbes to withstand antimicrobials. These genetic modifications can also cause non-selected changes in other cell phenotypes, such as fitness and susceptibility to antibiotic classes different from the one under selection. These collateral effects of AMR acquisition could be exploited to improve treatments. This is increasingly important in light of AMR as a major global health problem, associated with 4.71 million deaths worldwide in 2021, with 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to AMR. Additionally, the lack of development of novel antimicrobials active against resistant infections continues to compound the crisis. Even if new antimicrobials are developed, resistance will most likely emerge through adaptive evolution. Therefore, it is imperative to explore strategies to maintain the efficacy of new and existing antibiotics and limit the acquisition of AMR to continue to treat infections successfully. Understanding the impact of resistance acquisition on the bacterial phenotype, including collateral effects, has the potential to improve therapeutic outcomes. In this perspective, we will summarize the collateral effects of resistance acquisition, including fitness costs, collateral susceptibility networks, mutant selection windows and the probability of establishment of bacterial populations, and explore how these may be exploited to enhance the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. We will also discuss how challenges such as genetic background, polymicrobial infections and the environment are current barriers to the translation of these principles into the clinic.

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila, and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: Abstract Glycolipids are major components of the mycobacterial cell envelope and play critical roles in host-pathogen interactions. Here we investigate the capacity of the mycobacterial glycolipid phosphatidyl-myo-inositol hexamannosides (PIM 6 ) to modulate innate responsiveness in naive primary human monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs). Monocytes and MDMs prestimulated with PIM6, followed by 5 days of rest, secreted attenuated levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 6 (IL-6), and interleukin 10 (IL-10) following LPS challenge. PIM 6 pretreatment significantly altered pattern recognition receptor expression through the experimental time course and programmed a tolerized phenotype in myeloid cells independent of TLR2 activity. In an infection challenge with H37Rv Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), MDMs pretreated with PIM 6 secreted decreased levels of TNF-α and IL-10 and exhibited early increased bacterial control. Together, these data reveal PIM 6 as a complex immunomodulator that tolerizes myeloid cells to subsequent stimuli and exerts direct effects on the control of M.tb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring. We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco. We retrospectively analyzed 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes performed from April 2022 to July 2026 and linked available Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra results with target-level molecular outputs. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was detected in 203 episodes (78.7%), of which 188 (92.6%) had an interpretable rifampicin result. Molecular rifampicin resistance was detected in 75/188 episodes (39.9%) and isoniazid resistance in 71/192 (37.0%); molecular multidrug-resistant tuberculosis was identified in 51/184 (27.7%) episodes with paired results. Among 186 episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 21/112 (18.8%) rifampicin-susceptible and 54/74 (73.0%) rifampicin-resistant episodes. Among 92 resistant episodes with complete profiles, 66 (71.7%) showed resistance to two or more drug classes. rpoB3- and rpoB4- associated signals predominated among rifampicin-resistant episodes, katG -associated signals among isoniazid-resistant episodes, and gyrA targets among fluoroquinolone-resistant episodes. Mixed wild-type and mutation-associated signals occurred across rpoB and gyrA . These findings support the use of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing as a component of regional drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance, enabling systematic characterization of multiclass resistance and molecular resistance patterns within routine diagnostic networks. Such molecular surveillance should be integrated with phenotypic susceptibility testing and genomic sequencing to resolve discordant, atypical, or clinically consequential profiles and build a more comprehensive regional resistance-monitoring system.

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a phylogeny-guided graph attention network approach, coupled with a novel method for converting SNP-annotated phylogenetic trees into graph structures suitable for graph neural network processing. Results Using a dataset of 1000 M. tuberculosis isolates, representing the four main lineages, and 206 single-nucleotide variants (75 resistance-associated and 131 neutral) spanning 79 drug-resistance genes, we constructed graphs where nodes represented individual isolates and edges reflected phylogenetic distances. To reduce noise and highlight local evolutionary structure, we pruned edges between isolates separated by more than seven internal nodes. Node features were encoded as binary indicators of SNP presence or absence, and the graph attention network (GAT) architecture comprised two attention layers with a residual connection, followed by global attention pooling and a multilayer perceptron classifier. The model achieved higher accuracy (0.81, AUC 0.82) than a homoplasy-count baseline (0.71) on the held-out test set. Under repeated cross-validation, however, F1 scores did not differ significantly (0.56 vs. 0.58; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.98), reflecting a specificity-sensitivity trade-off: the GAT favoured specificity (0.89), the baseline favoured sensitivity. Applying the model to 138 WHO-classified “uncertain” variants identified 28 high-confidence candidates, including rpoC Ile491Val (rifampicin, compensatory), ubiA Arg240Cys (ethambutol), and rpsA Ala412Val (pyrazinamide). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of encoding phylogenetic trees as graph neural network-compatible structures and the utility of attention-based models for detecting positive-selection signals, supporting genomic surveillance and prioritisation of candidates for experimental validation. Availability and Implementation The source code for the model can be found at https://github.com/linfeng-wang/Phylogeny-Guided_GAT .

research.abstract: Immunomodulatory Activity of Galing Leaf Extract and Fraction (Cayratia trifolia L) Against Specific Immune Response in ESAT-6 TB-Induced Diabetes Mellit us Rats The immune system protects the body against infections. However, in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), impaired immune function increases the risk of developing active tuberculosis (TB). CD4+ T cell activation is essential for controlling Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, but immune system dysfunction in DM makes the body more susceptible to infection. Natural immunomodulators are promising therapeutic alternatives because they may have fewer side effects and can enhance immune responses. Galing (Cayratia trifolia L.) is known to contain bioactive compounds with antidiabetic, antibacterial, and immunomodulatory activities. This study aimed to investigate the potential of Galing leaf extract and fractions to enhance the CD4+-mediated specific immune response in an animal model of DM induced with the TB antigen ESAT-6. Dried plant material was macerated using 96% ethanol, followed by evaporation to obtain the ethanolic extract. Fractionation was then performed using vacuum liquid chromatography (VLC) with a gradient elution system, yielding five fractions. Immunomodulatory activity was evaluated by measuring CD4+ levels using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The experimental animals were divided into nine groups: normal control, negative control, positive control, fractions 1-5, and extract, with a dose of 50 mg/kg body weight administered to each treatment group. The immunomodulatory assay results showed CD4+ levels of 8.399 μg/mL in fraction 1, 8.047 μg/mL in fraction 2, 6.490 μg/mL in fraction 3, 6.492 μg/mL in fraction 4, 5.917 μg/mL in fraction 5, and 7.284 μg/mL in the extract group. The findings indicated that Galing leaf extract and fractions could enhance the specific immune response by increasing CD4+ levels. Galing demonstrated immunomodulatory activity, with fractions 1 and 2 showing the greatest efficacy (p < 0.05). In conclusion, Galing leaf extract and fractions have potential as natural immunomodulatory agents to enhance CD4+ mediated immune responses in an animal model of DM induced with the TB antigen ESAT-6. research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

research.abstract: Background Genomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized. We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples. Methods In this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health. We compared clade proportions and dynamics, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values between clinical and community samples. Findings We analyzed 538 RSV sequences collected between 2019 and 2021 (278 community, 260 clinical), 1506 influenza sequences (260 community, 1246 clinical) between 2019 and 2020, and 8660 SARS-CoV-2 sequences (5923 community, 2737 clinical) from 2020 to 2022. Clade proportions did not differ between clinical and community samples for RSV or influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2: clades 21J (Delta) and 21K (Omicron BA.1) were more frequent in community samples and clade 22B (Omicron BA.5) in clinical samples. SARS-CoV-2 clinical sequence clusters were more diverse than community clusters, whereas RSV and influenza showed no significant difference. Several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples for SARS-CoV-2. Ct values were lower in clinical samples for multiple SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza clades. Interpretation Seasonal respiratory viruses had similar dynamics and diversity in clinical and community samples, whereas pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differed between settings. Genomic surveillance programs should combine clinical and community sampling, particularly during pandemics in order to better capture viral diversity.

research.abstract: Abstract Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman ρ=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated SPP1 -enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

research.abstract: Abstract Phylum Actinomycetota (syn. Actinobacteriota or Actinobacteria), one of the largest well-studied bacterial phyla, is renowned for complex morphology, non-motility, ecological versatility, and secondary metabolite production. Chemosensory systems (CSS) are among the most sophisticated prokaryotic signal transduction architectures, yet their evolutionary distribution in this phylum remains poorly understood. Here, a comparative genomic analysis of 693 high-quality genomes spanning the phylum resolves the diversity, distribution, and evolutionary trajectories of CSS. Despite extensive genomic complexity and ecological versatility, only 6.9% of genomes encode complete CSS clusters, confined to a subset of lineages within a few classes, indicating lineage-specific retention or loss. In contrast, two-component systems (TCS) are ubiquitously abundant, with hybrid kinases enriched in CSS-deficient classes, suggesting functional compensation for the absence of dedicated chemosensory pathways. Basal lineages retain simplified CSS (F1 or F5), whereas Actinomycetes show lineage-specific expansion into multiple classes (F5, F8, F9, and ACF), often co-occurring, indicative of enhanced sensory complexity. The phylogeny of CheA homologs shows a polyphyletic distribution, supporting a mosaic evolutionary history shaped by multiple independent acquisitions, diversification, and gene loss. Collectively, our findings show that, unlike motile bacteria, Actinomycetota members rely predominantly on TCS-driven regulatory networks, with CSS retained only in select lineages where ecological demands require enhanced environmental sensing. This work provides a phylum-wide evolutionary framework for the emergence, diversification, and functional specialization of CSS in non-motile bacteria. Importance Bacteria rely on sensory signal transduction systems to detect and respond to environmental changes. Chemosensory systems typically control movement along with alternate cellular functions, but their role in non-motile phylum Actinomycetota has remained unclear. By analyzing approximately seven hundred Actinobacterial genomes, we report that these systems are rare and restricted to specific lineages, suggesting they are retained only where they confer ecological advantages. In contrast, most Actinomycetota depend on alternative signaling pathways, particularly two-component systems, for environmental adaptation. These findings highlight how different bacterial groups evolve distinct strategies for sensing and responding to their surroundings, providing new insights into microbial evolution, ecological specialization, and the emergence of complex adaptive traits.

research.abstract: Abstract Deep-sea hydrothermal vents and methane seeps host unique animal communities sustained by chemosynthetic symbioses, yet how biological diversification proceeds across these geochemically distinct and geographically fragmented habitats remains poorly understood. Previous studies have largely focused on either host genomic adaptation or symbiont diversity as drivers of isolation, leaving unresolved how environmental geochemistry and host–microbe associations jointly shape evolutionary trajectories in chemosynthetic ecosystems. Here, we addressed this gap by combining chromosome-level host genomics, population resequencing, and episymbiont metagenomics in the deep-sea chemosynthetic lobster Shinkaia crosnieri, a dominant species inhabiting both hydrothermal vents and methane seeps. Genomic innovations—including sensory tradeoffs (vision loss versus chemosensory expansion), metabolic compensation for pigment loss, and positive selection on respiratory protein—underpin deep-sea colonization of S. crosnieri. Populations from the Okinawa Trough vent and the South China Sea seep exhibit pronounced genetic divergence, potentially driven by Pleistocene vicariance and reinforced by divergent selection across sulfur-enriched (vent) versus sulfur-depleted, methane-dominated (seep) environments. This selection targets host genes involved in chemoreception and immunity, with coordinated signatures in both sequence evolution and structural variation. Crucially, holobiont-level adaptation is amplified by habitat-specific recruitment of episymbionts: sulfur-oxidizing Campylobacterales/Thiotrichales dominate vent-associated lobsters, while methanotrophic Methylococcales prevail at seep counterparts. These symbionts partition energy niches metabolically, with seep-associated communities enhancing biosynthesis of key cofactors (e.g. coenzyme Q, tetrahydrofolate). Host transporters for these nutrients are concurrently upregulated, demonstrating functional synergy. Our findings establish that diversification in extreme environments operates holobiont-wide, where geochemical gradients synergistically shape host genomic plasticity and symbiont metabolic specialization to drive early-stage divergence.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT China's complex river basins constitute a critical biogeographic setting for investigating genetic differentiation and lineage divergence in freshwater fishes. Opsariichthys bidens is broadly distributed among multiple, hydrologically isolated river basins, rendering it a well‐suited system for assessing mitochondrial phylogeographic structure across major river basins. Here, we used newly generated mitochondrial data to characterize broad‐scale genetic variation in O. bidens across China's major river basins. We analyzed 379 cytochrome b ( cyt b ) sequences sampled from 13 geographically distinct populations, including seven populations from the Yangtze River and one population from each of six other major rivers, complemented by complete mitochondrial genomes from one individual from each population. Mitochondrial diversity was high at the species level (haplotype diversity, H d = 0.942; nucleotide diversity, π = 0.02526), but varied markedly among populations, with some populations showing haplotype fixation and others retaining divergent haplotypes. Genetic differentiation was pronounced, with 83.84% of variation attributable to differences among populations; 93.6% of pairwise F st values exceeded 0.25. Haplotype‐network and phylogenetic analyses showed two deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages, broadly distributed in northern and southern China, respectively, with further substructure broadly associated with major river basins. Complete mitochondrial genomes exhibited high structural conservation across lineages, and the clearest lineage‐associated annotation differences were observed in the termination codons of nd1 and cox3 . Overall, these results provide a broad‐scale mitochondrial phylogeographic assessment of O. bidens and reveal a general association between river‐basin geography and mitochondrial lineage structure across China.

research.abstract: A bstract S ummary We present BlastPhyMe (BLAST, Phylogenies, and Molecular Evolution) a new application to facilitate the fast and easy generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets. The application uses a portable database framework to manage and organize sequences along with a graphical user interface (GUI) that makes the application extremely easy to use. BlastPhyMe utilizes several existing services and applications in a unique way that saves researchers considerable time when building and analyzing protein-coding datasets. The application consists of two modules that can be used separately or together. The first module enables the assembly of coding sequence datasets. BLAST searches can be used to obtain all related sequences of interest from NCBI. Full GenBank records are saved within the database and coding sequences are automatically extracted. A feature of particular note is that sequences can be sorted based on NCBI taxonomic hierarchy before export export in formats such as FASTA for visualization using existing tools, such as MEGA. The application provides GUIs for automatic alignment of sequences with the popular tools MUSCLE and PRANK, as well as for reconstructing phylogenetic trees using PhyML. The second module incorporates selection analyses using codon-based likelihood methods. The alignments and phylogenetic trees generated with the dataset module, or those generated elsewhere, can be used to run the models implemented in the codeml PAML package. A GUI allows easy selection of models and parameters. Importantly, replicate analyses with different parameter starting values can be automatically performed in order to ensure selection of the best-fitting model. Multiple analyses can be run simultaneously based on the number of processor cores available, while additional analyses will be run iteratively until completed. Results are saved within the database and can be exported to publication-ready Excel tables, which further automatically compute the appropriate likelihood ratio test between models in order to determine statistical significance. Future development will expand the available phylogenetic and molecular-evolutionary analyses. BlastPhyMe saves researchers of all bioinformatics experience levels considerable time by automating the numerous tasks required for the generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets using a straightforward graphical interface. research.abstract: Abstract The evolution of pesticide resistance in herbivores poses a significant challenge in agriculture. A refuge strategy, where farmers plant non-toxin-treated plants to promote growth of susceptible herbivore individuals near treated plants and facilitate gene exchange between susceptible and resistant individuals, has been used in resistance management. However, we know very little about the effect of spatiotemporal fluctuations in selection pressure on resistance management. Furthermore, pests show oviposition preference and assortative mating behaviours, both of which have rarely been considered by researchers when designing resistance management strategies. Using a stochastic eco-evolutionary plant-herbivore model, we show that over a wide range of population parameters, directional changes in toxicity level and refuge frequency that reduce selection pressure for the resistance allele in the initial pest generations are much more effective for resistance management than exposing pests to a constant toxicity level and refuge frequency across pest generations. However, the exact magnitude of the effect of changing toxicity and refuge frequency relative to keeping them constant across pest generations is sensitive to underlying population parameter values. Our results show that the refuge strategy is most effective when niche choice can evolve, but assortative mating shows both negative and positive effects in resistance management. Thus, our results reveal a potential mechanism underlying the refuge strategy’s successes in the field. We show how resistance allele dominance and resistance costs influence our observations, and discuss our results in the context of partial protection from directional selection and field resistance management.

research.abstract: Background: Thyroid dysfunction is a common endocrine comorbidity in type 1 diabetes (T1D), yet most evidence on its burden and biochemical patterns comes from higher-income settings. Data among African children and young adults with T1D remain limited. Objective: To determine the prevalence and pattern of thyroid dysfunction and examine demographic and diabetes-related factors associated with thyroid dysfunction among children and young adults with T1D in Kenya. Methods: We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among children and young adults with T1D aged [≤]34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4) were measured. Thyroid status was classified as euthyroidism (normal TSH and FT4), subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal FT4), overt hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with low FT4), subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH with normal FT4), overt hyperthyroidism (low TSH with elevated FT4), or discordant TSH-FT4 profiles that did not meet these predefined biochemical categories. Prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and multivariable logistic regression examined associations with age, sex and duration of diabetes. Results: Among 244 participants with paired TSH and FT4 measurements, 77.5% (n=189) were euthyroid. Twenty-seven participants (11.1%; 95% CI 7.7-15.6%) had biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction: 18 (7.4%) had subclinical hypothyroidism, 5 (2.0%) overt hypothyroidism, and 4 (1.6%) subclinical hyperthyroidism. No overt hyperthyroidism was identified. An additional 28 participants (11.5%) had discordant TSH-FT4 profiles. Hypothyroidism accounted for 85.2% of biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction and was predominantly subclinical (78.3%). Age, sex and duration of diabetes were not significantly associated with thyroid dysfunction in adjusted analyses. Conclusion: Thyroid dysfunction affected approximately one in nine Kenyan children and young adults with T1D and was predominantly hypothyroid, particularly subclinical hypothyroidism. Discordant TSH-FT4 profiles were also frequent, underscoring the importance of careful biochemical classification and confirmation of abnormal thyroid-function tests.

research.abstract: Background Anterior chest wall tuberculosis is an uncommon form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that can mimic a chronic pyogenic abscess or chest wall mass. Its indolent presentation and absence of constitutional symptoms may delay diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. Case presentation A 22-year-old previously healthy male soldier presented with a progressively enlarging parasternal-xiphoid swelling and intermittent seropurulent discharge, without respiratory or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed a minimally tender 5 × 2 cm fluctuant swelling with a draining sinus and localized skin changes. Thoracic computed tomography showed a 57 × 18 mm subcutaneous collection at the xiphoid level without demonstrated pleural or osseous involvement, alongside centrilobular nodules and a tree-in-bud pattern suggestive of pulmonary infection. Incision, drainage, and debridement were performed. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing of a fluid specimen detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex at a low bacillary load, without rifampicin resistance detected. Histopathological examination was reported to show caseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Sputum testing was also positive for M. tuberculosis, supporting concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis. First-line antituberculous therapy was initiated. The wound was closed at the 14-day postoperative assessment. Following six months of treatment, the patient remained asymptomatic; follow-up computed tomography demonstrated resolution of the chest wall collection and regression of pulmonary abnormalities. Conclusion Chest wall tuberculosis should be considered in patients with persistent parasternal swelling or a draining sinus, even without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Tissue sampling, molecular and histopathological evaluation, and assessment for concomitant pulmonary disease support timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an escalating global public health concern, contributing significantly to global mortalities and posing a major financial burden, particularly in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) like Ghana [Letsa, 2023]. Suboptimal quality of care can lead to severe microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy (DN) and opportunistic infections like urinary tract infections (UTIs) [Letsa, 2023]. DN affects 30–40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, with a reported prevalence of kidney diseases of 12.5% in Ghana [Adoba et al., 2025]. Given that monitoring quality of care is crucial for prevention, this study aimed to evaluate the quality of DM care indicators, particularly focusing on urinary biomarkers, at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital. Methodology A cross-sectional design employing a retrospective medical audit was utilized, assessing patient records at the GPHA hospital Diabetes Clinic. The study population comprised 125 participants whose urinalysis data, demographics, and comorbidity categorization (Diabetes only, Diabetes and Hypertension, Diabetes and Cyesis, etc.) were collected. Urine parameters, including albuminuria, glucose, and Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC), were retrieved from Sysmex’s urinalysis analyzers (Sysmex UC 400, UF 350). Results The study cohort consisted predominantly of females (58.4%, n=73) with a mean age of 54.92 years. The primary diabetic categorization was “diabetes only” (76.8%, n=96). Evaluation of albuminuria showed that mild albuminuria was recorded for only 10.4% (n=13) of participants, and overt albuminuria was absent (0.0%). This mild albuminuria prevalence is notably below the 25–30% global prevalence reported for type 2 diabetics. A significant correlation was established between the various diabetes population categories and urine glucose (Pr=0.001). Pathological RTEC results (> 2.5) were identified in three individuals, primarily from the diabetes and hypertension category (2 individuals) and the diabetes and cyesis category (1 individual). The study noted limitations, including the difficulty in acquiring the specific type of diabetes and the non-availability of data on medication type or complication level. Conclusion The prevalence of mild albuminuria among the study population at the GPHA hospital was significantly lower than established global and certain regional Ghanaian rates. However, the detection of a significant association between diabetic categorization and glucosuria underscores the need for continuous and rigorous monitoring of renal function markers. These findings suggest that while indicators like mild albuminuria may be lower than expected in this specific cohort, targeted interventions remain essential to prevent the progression of renal complications in this high-risk population [ Adoba et al., 2025].

research.abstract: Abstract Objective To assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. Methods We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. Findings Among 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. In Survey B, interest varied according to lived TB experience, with FGDs suggesting that previous negative experiences with injectables may have contributed to this variation. Conclusion Interest in LAIs for TB treatment and prevention was high, but lower among participants with lived TB experience. Product development and implementation should address concerns about injectables and side effects while preserving patient choice and agency.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: The intersection of tuberculosis (TB) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a major global health challenge. Although T2DM is a recognized risk factor for active TB, its epidemiological impact on latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and the underlying immune mechanisms remain unclear. This meta-analysis estimated the global prevalence of LTBI in T2DM, compared LTBI risk with non-diabetic controls, and evaluated the roles of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) in immune dysregulation. HbA1c and IFN-γ were selected because they represent the gold-standard indicators of long-term glycemic control and IGRA-based immune responses, respectively. A systematic search identified observational studies using interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) to diagnose LTBI in T2DM patients. Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation was performed to calculate pooled prevalence, odds ratios (ORs), mean differences (MDs) for HbA1c, and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for IFN-γ levels. Ten studies involving 1,740 T2DM patients and non-diabetic controls were included. The pooled LTBI prevalence in T2DM was 27% (95% CI: 23%–32%; I² = 76%). Compared with non-diabetic individuals, T2DM patients had an 86% higher risk of LTBI (OR 1.86; 95% CI: 1.41–2.45; p<0.0001; I² = 0%). T2DM patients with LTBI also showed poorer glycemic control, with HbA1c levels 0.75% higher than those without LTBI (MD 0.75; 95% CI: 0.51–0.99; p<0.00001; I² = 0%). Furthermore, T2DM was associated with significantly reduced Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific IFN-γ production (SMD −1.93; 95% CI: −2.69 to −1.16; p<0.00001; I² = 78%). These findings indicate that T2DM substantially increases LTBI risk through hyperglycemia-associated immune dysregulation and impaired Th1-mediated IFN-γ responses. Routine LTBI screening using IGRA and optimal glycemic control should be integrated into diabetes management to reduce progression to active TB.
